notes:
I found good material for most verses, but some of what you asked for isn't there. I found no clear disagreement between Protestant traditions on this chapter. The closest things are a Reformed note on worship at v. 5 and a difference over whether repentance was still possible at v. 11. I found nothing from Lutheran, Orthodox or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace sources, so those are left out. One more thing: Guzik's Enduring Word page has an AI-written summary at the top. I used it only where it matches his commentary below it.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** This scene follows on from the potter's house in ch. 18. There the clay could still be reshaped. Here the pot has been fired and hardened, so it can only be broken. God showed him how the potter could mold clay again into a new shape if it should seem resistant. Here, the clay is baked, hardened, and breakable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Ellicott says the Hebrew word for the jar, *bakbuk*, is meant to sound like water gurgling out. The word for "vessel" indicates a large earthen jar with a narrow neck. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-1.htm
- The elders were there as witnesses. Ellicott says they represented the civil and religious rulers, the witnesses of this acted prophecy of the destruction of all that they held most precious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes how cheap and fragile ordinary pottery in Palestine was. It adds that this message concerned the whole people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** ch. 18 showed God's power as a potter. Here the point is that a vessel which is finished and splendid can still be broken. He says Jeremiah stressed this so the Jews could not claim their state under David's line would last forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/19-1.html
- **Matthew Henry:** He finds it striking that leading men would follow a poor prophet out of the city without knowing why. His lesson is that people of high rank honour God by attending to His word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_019.cfm
- Coffman reads more into the jar: it was earthen (Israel's humble origins), finely made (her past glory) and fragile (her weakness). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/19-1.html

**v. 2**
- **Potsherd Gate:** Pulpit says this was where broken pottery was thrown. It links the gate's name to what Jeremiah does there, but says its location is uncertain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says the gate may be the same as Nehemiah's "Dung Gate," which led into this valley. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm
- Guzik describes the valley as a rubbish dump with fires always smouldering, earlier used for child sacrifice. He says this made it a vivid picture of the fate of the damned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Matthew Henry: God's word is not tied to one place, and as good a sermon may be preached in the valley of Tophet as in the gate of the temple. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_019.cfm

**v. 3**
- **"Kings" (plural):** Keil & Delitzsch say the word is plural because the sins of the reigning king's successors were also in view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-1.htm
- Guzik, quoting Feinberg, says the message was aimed at the whole dynasty responsible for the apostasy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Pulpit, by contrast, takes "kings" to mean the many royal princes, kings "by courtesy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- "Ears will ring" echoes 2 Kings 21:12 and 1 Samuel 3:11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Joseph Benson (Methodist): the report alone would astonish anyone who heard it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/19-5.html

**v. 4**
- **"Made this a foreign place":** Pulpit reads it as treating the place as if it did not belong to God, as unholy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Guzik, quoting Thompson, says the place had been so changed it could no longer be recognised as Israelite. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Wesley (Methodist): "this place" may mean the city or the valley. Either way, they had turned it to a use quite contrary to what God gave it for. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/19.htm
- **"Blood of the innocent" – the commentators disagree:**
  - Pulpit takes it as the children sacrificed to Moloch, citing Psalm 106:38. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch reject that. They take it as judicial murder or persecution of the godly, echoing Manasseh in 2 Kings 21:16. They see the list of sins rising to a climax: idolatry, then bloodshed, then child sacrifice as the worst of all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-5.htm
  - The Cambridge Bible agrees with Keil: the verse means innocent people in general, not children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 5**
- **Baal and Molech:** Pulpit thinks "Baal" is used loosely here for Moloch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Wesley says Baal ("lord") and Molech ("king") mean the same thing and seem to be general names for idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/19.htm
- **Real burning, not just a ritual:** Guzik quotes Kidner: these verses leave no doubt that these were actual burnt-offerings, although not burnt alive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Gill also says the text is clear that the children were actually burned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-5.htm
- **"Never entered My mind":** Guzik says the practice went totally against God's nature. He reads Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22) as God's emphatic way of saying He does not want human sacrifice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown add that God did more than not command it: He commanded the opposite (Leviticus 18:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-5.htm
- **Reformed reading (Geneva Bible note):** The words show that whatever God's word does not command about His worship is against His word. This is the closest thing to a tradition-specific reading I found. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/19-5.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) describes babies placed on red-hot metal idols of Baal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/19-1.html
- Bible.org suggests some may have misused Genesis 22:2 or Exodus 13 as "proof-texts" for these sacrifices. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-19
- **Popular modern application (Bible Hub Q&A):** It applies the verse to legalised killing of the innocent and to protecting life from conception. https://biblehub.com/q/Jeremiah_19_5_God_s_character_justice.htm
- That page also says digs in the Hinnom Valley have found infant bones. I couldn't check this against any scholarly source, so treat it with care. https://biblehub.com/q/Jeremiah_19_5_God_s_character_justice.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: this repeats the warning of Jeremiah 7:32. There would be a terrible slaughter in that valley. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- The Cambridge Bible calls verses 5–6 substantially the same as 7:31–32. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 7**
- **"Ruin the plans":** In Hebrew this is a wordplay. The verb literally means "pour out" or "empty," the same root as the word for the jar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Some think Jeremiah poured the jar out on the ground as he spoke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Wesley: God would defeat every plan they made to escape His judgments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/19.htm
- Guzik, quoting Harrison: leaving bodies unburied horrified the Hebrews. Ironically, their sanctuary would become their cemetery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/

**v. 8**
- Pulpit links this verse to Jeremiah 18:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Guzik: the disaster would show both in the people's deaths and in the city's ruin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/

**v. 9**
- This almost word for word repeats the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:53. Lamentations 4:10 records it coming true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Guzik compares the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/

**v. 10**
- Bible.org: in ch. 18 the clay could be remade, but fired clay can only be destroyed. It says there was no hope of repentance on Judah's part or YHWH's part. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-19
- The Cambridge Bible quotes Thomson on a local custom of smashing a jar behind someone to call down hopeless ruin on them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 11**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik: the jar would break quickly and completely, and so would Judah. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: finding tolerance of sin in God's saving purpose is the most terrible of evils. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: no cleverness could repair the ruin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-19.html
- **A different note on hope:** Matthew Henry agrees no human hand could repair it, but adds that if they return to the Lord he will heal. Compare Bible.org's "no hope" at v. 10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/19.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** Pulpit and Cambridge say the words "bury in Topheth" seem out of place here, are missing in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), and were added from 7:32. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 12**
- "Like Topheth" means an unclean place that people avoid (Pulpit). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- Wesley: a place of slaughter and burials. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/19.htm
- The Cambridge Bible: Josiah had made Topheth unclean (2 Kings 23:10), and Jerusalem's houses would become the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 13**
- Rooftops were used for feasts, meetings, and prayer. They had become places for star worship (cf. Zephaniah 1:5; Jeremiah 32:29). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm
- Pulpit: the received Hebrew is hard to translate here. The KJV quietly changed it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 14**
- Wesley: Jeremiah went back by God's direction to the temple court, which was open to all, where the most might hear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/19.htm
- Pulpit sees a new section starting here: the warning repeated before all the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** Cambridge thinks this passage comes from Baruch's memoirs of Jeremiah, since the prophet is in the third person. It treats vv. 3–9 as a later editorial addition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/19.htm

**v. 15**
- **"Stiffened their necks":** Guzik says Judah's greatest sin was refusing to hear God's word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- Matthew Henry: sinners' hardness is their own fault. He urges prayer to be kept from hardness of heart, and contempt of his word and commandments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/19.htm
- He also warns against assuming God's threats are only meant to frighten. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_019.cfm
- "All her towns": the cities of Judah are seen as under the capital (Pulpit). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/19.htm

**Background across the chapter (Catholic and others)**
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** Ahaz and Manasseh set up Baal-Moloch worship at Topheth. Josiah defiled it, in spite of which Joakim restored there the infamous worship of Moloch. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08344a.htm
- It also explains how Ge Hinnom became "Gehenna," the emblem of hell. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08344a.htm
- Guzik makes the same link to Jesus' word *Gehenna*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-19/
- A NET Bible dictionary entry (ISBE) says where the valley actually lies is still uncertain. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=GEHENNA
